findings.issue_text: [BUG] The sed invocation uses BSD-only `sed -i ''` syntax, which fails on GNU sed (Linux): `sed -i '' -E "s|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=$TUNNEL_URL|" "$ENV_FILE"` treats the empty string as a file operand, so sed errors with "can't read : No such file or directory" and never performs the substitution. On Linux, the GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL in .env is never updated, but because the script has no `set -e`, execution continues and prints "✅ Updated GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL in ../.env" — the developer proceeds testing gcal webhooks against a stale/missing webhook URL.

[BUG] ENV_FILE is hardcoded as the CWD-relative path `../.env`, which only resolves to the repo root .env if the script is invoked from inside scripts/ — running it the conventional way from the repo root (`bash scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh`) resolves `../.env` to a file one level above the repository. A developer running the script from the repo root gets their .env created/edited outside the repo (or a spurious file at an unrelated path), while the in-repo .env that the dev server reads is never updated; combined with the success message the script prints, the webhook URL appears configured when it is not.

[ADVISORY] The handler constructs `new CalendarCacheRepository()` directly instead of going through the calendar-cache dependency-injection/selection mechanism that calendar-cache.repository.mock.ts exists for, and issues the groupBy unconditionally on every connectedCalendars request. In environments where calendar-cache is disabled or substituted with the mock (e.g. E2E runs, cache-disabled deployments), the mock's documented contract ('Skipping getCacheStatusByCredentialIds due to calendar-cache being disabled') is bypassed and the real DB groupBy runs anyway — every connectedCalendars fetch pays an extra query, and test setups relying on the mock substitution stop intercepting cache calls made through this path.

[BUG] The handler instantiates `new CalendarCacheRepository()` directly instead of going through the feature-flag-gated repository selection that `calendar-cache.repository.mock.ts` exists for, so the calendarCache groupBy query and the resulting cache-status serialization run even when the calendar-cache feature is disabled. Deployments with calendar-cache disabled pay an extra DB query per connectedCalendars request, and users are shown a 'Cache Status' / 'Delete cached data' UI for a feature that is supposed to be off; deleting then mutates cache rows through a path the flag was meant to gate. This is the sibling-flag miss: the touched serialization path is gated by the calendar-cache flag, and the gate is not checked at the new call site.

[BUG] The handler throws a plain `Error("Credential not found or access denied")` instead of a TRPCError, so tRPC masks the message and the client receives a generic 500 INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR rather than a 4xx distinguishing not-found from access-denied. A user submitting a stale or forged credentialId gets an 'Error deleting cache' toast caused by a 500, and operators cannot distinguish authorization failures from server faults in logs/monitoring; the handler's carefully-worded error message never reaches any client.

[BUG] `hasCache = isGoogleCalendar && cacheUpdatedAt` does not exclude delegation credentials the way `canDisconnect` does, so the 'Delete cached data' action is offered for workspace-delegated Google connections whose cache is shared across the organization, while the same connections are deliberately blocked from disconnect. Any org member viewing their delegated Google connection can delete the org-wide delegated calendar cache, degrading availability freshness for every member until the next refresh; the component encodes two different trust policies (canDisconnect vs hasCache) for the same credential row without reconciling them.

[BUG] `updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` executes unconditionally after the conditional fetch-and-set-cache branch, bumping SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for every calendar under the credential even on runs where no cache entry was written, so SelectedCalendar.updatedAt no longer reflects an actual cache refresh. Any consumer of SelectedCalendar.updatedAt (the field is now selected in UserRepository and getConnectedDestinationCalendars) reads a 'last updated' timestamp that advances on every availability fetch cycle regardless of whether cached data changed, defeating the purpose of the timestamp this PR introduces.

[ADVISORY] The new per-credential write is dead weight in this diff: the UI's 'Last updated' status is computed from CalendarCache.updatedAt via getCacheStatusByCredentialIds, not from SelectedCalendar.updatedAt, and no code in this diff reads the bumped value. Every calendar-cache refresh cycle performs an extra write to all SelectedCalendar rows of the credential whose result is not consumed by any reader here — pure hot-path write cost, and the next maintainer must reverse-engineer why a no-data updateMany exists at all.

[ADVISORY] The mutation queries and deletes via raw `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany`, bypassing the ICalendarCacheRepository abstraction that every other cache operation (including the new getCacheStatusByCredentialIds) goes through. The cache-mutation path has no disabled-mode mock counterpart and no single place-to-update: any future change to cache deletion semantics (e.g., also clearing channels or honoring the feature flag) must now be made in two layers, and the repository interface silently diverges from actual usage.

[ADVISORY] The timestamp is formatted with a hardcoded `Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)` while the component imports `useLocale` for translations, so the locale used for text and the locale used for the timestamp diverge. Non-English users see their cache status sentence in their language but the timestamp in US month/day/year format — a visible i18n inconsistency on the very screen this PR adds; the fix (passing the locale from useLocale) is trivial and is what the sibling code elsewhere in the app does.

[ADVISORY] `updatedAt` and `googleChannelId` are added to the selectedCalendars select of a widely-used user query, but no code in this diff consumes either field from this select (the UI's cacheUpdatedAt comes from the CalendarCache groupBy in connectedCalendars.handler). Every user fetch across the app now transfers two additional columns per selected calendar with no consumer in this changeset — either the enrichment was half-wired (the status should have been derived from these fields and isn't) or the fields are speculative additions that should not ship on this hot path.

[BUG] No automated test exists anywhere in this diff for the new behavior-bearing logic: the deleteCache mutation (ownership check + delete), getCacheStatusByCredentialIds, the connectedCalendars enrichment, or CredentialActionsDropdown's gating conditions. The ownership check in deleteCache is the only thing preventing a user from deleting another tenant's calendar cache rows; a regression there (e.g., dropping the userId filter or reordering the where clause) ships silently. Evidence of absence: the diff was scanned for test-shaped files (spec/**, test/**, *.spec.*, *_test.go, test_*.py) and contains none; scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh is a manual tunnel-setup dev script, not an automated test, and assertions on the mock's new getCacheStatusByCredentialIds method exist nowhere.

[BUG] A new 79-line Tunnelmole-based Google webhook testing script is shipped inside a PR whose stated intent is calendar cache status and actions, with zero traceability to any requirement in the feature. The PR's review surface, merge risk, and repo footprint expand with unrelated dev tooling: the script mutates ../.env via BSD-only 'sed -i '' -E' (silently fails or corrupts on Linux CI/dev machines) and is entirely unmaintained by the feature it rides in with; reviewers approving cache-status work are unknowingly approving a webhook-tunneling utility.

[BUG] The dev:cron script change from 'ts-node cron-tester.ts' to 'npx tsx cron-tester.ts' is unrelated tooling churn not traceable to the calendar-cache-status requirement, and 'npx tsx' resolves tsx at invocation time rather than via a declared dependency. A developer running 'yarn dev:cron' on a machine without tsx installed gets an npx interactive install prompt or a different tsx version than the repo pins, breaking the cron test loop; this change belongs in a separate tooling PR where it can be reviewed against its own motivation.

[ADVISORY] The refactor of findMany drops the 'satisfies Prisma.SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs' compile-time check, an unrelated change bundled into the cache-status feature that removes type validation of where/select/orderBy against the Prisma API surface. The next caller of SelectedCalendarRepository.findMany can pass a malformed where or select clause that previously failed the build via satisfies and now only fails at runtime with a PrismaClientValidationError in production request paths; whoever makes that change gets no compile-time guard.

[ADVISORY] 'googleChannelId' is added to both SelectedCalendar pick types with no reader anywhere in this diff — it is implementation work not traceable to the cache-status requirement. Dead data-model surface: every future maintainer of UserWithCalendars must decide whether populating googleChannelId is required, and the field's presence implies a webhook-channel concern that this PR never implements; if it was added to satisfy a downstream consumer outside the diff, that dependency is undocumented and unreviewed.

[ADVISORY] UserRepository now selects 'updatedAt' and 'googleChannelId' for every user's selectedCalendars, but no code in this diff reads either field from this query path (the UI's cacheUpdatedAt comes from CalendarCache via connectedCalendars.handler). Unconditional payload growth on the user-query hot path for data with no consumer in this change; the shipped work is unverifiable against the requirement and will be flagged as dead by the next cleanup pass, or worse, silently load-bearing for code outside this diff.

[ADVISORY] The bulk updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {}) call on SelectedCalendar.updatedAt is not consumed by any UI or handler in this diff (the cache-status display reads CalendarCache.updatedAt instead), and it executes unconditionally even when the surrounding cache-write branch was skipped. Every availability fetch performs an extra DB write across all calendars under the credential for a value nobody reads, and because it sits outside the cache-write conditional it also fires on cache-skip paths — the requirement is met by CalendarCache.updatedAt alone, making this write untraceable dead work that still costs DB round-trips.

[ADVISORY] The disconnect flow (trpc.viewer.credentials.delete mutation, toast texts, cache invalidations, confirmation dialog) is a hand-maintained duplicate of the existing DisconnectIntegration component, which is not removed in this diff and still serves the same purpose elsewhere in the app. Two parallel implementations of app disconnection now exist: the next change to disconnect behavior (e.g. a new invalidation or audit hook) must be applied in both places or the two surfaces drift, and this component was introduced without a stated requirement to replace DisconnectIntegration globally.

[ADVISORY] The deleteCache mutation accepts any userId-owned credential and deletes its calendarCache rows without restricting to Google Calendar or checking the calendar-cache feature flag, while the UI gates the delete action to Google credentials only (isGoogleCalendar in CredentialActionsDropdown). An API consumer can invoke deleteCache against a non-Google credential and receive success:true after deleting whatever cache rows exist for it — a backend contract broader than the scoped feature, with no feature-flag guard so the destructive endpoint cannot be disabled independently of a code deploy.

[BUG] The new code calls SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {}) with an empty data object, which Prisma's updateMany rejects with PrismaClientValidationError ('at least one field must be set in data') because empty data is not a valid update input even when the goal is to trigger @updatedAt. Every invocation of fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache for Google Calendar throws at this line, so Google Calendar availability fetching fails for all users once this code path executes; even if a Prisma version tolerated empty data, the write fires unconditionally (including when the setAvailabilityInCache branch above was skipped), making it a wasted DB write per availability check on the booking hot path.

[ADVISORY] The handler directly instantiates `new CalendarCacheRepository()` instead of going through the selection mechanism that swaps in CalendarCacheRepositoryMock when the calendar-cache feature is disabled, so the feature flag no longer gates this read. Every connectedCalendars fetch issues a calendarCache groupBy against the DB even when the cache feature is off, and users are shown a 'Cache Status / Last updated' derived from stale rows that the disabled feature will never refresh — the parallel mock path added in this same diff (calendar-cache.repository.mock.ts) is dead code for this caller.

[ADVISORY] The design maintains two independent 'cache freshness' sources of truth: the UI status shown in this PR is read from CalendarCache.updatedAt (getCacheStatusByCredentialIds), while the writer added here bumps SelectedCalendar.updatedAt instead, and the diff also widens UserWithCalendars/UserRepository selects with SelectedCalendar.updatedAt and googleChannelId that no consumer in this diff reads. Two parallel freshness mechanisms that will drift: the SelectedCalendar update fires unconditionally on every availability fetch (even when nothing was cached because the cache branch was skipped), so it is decoupled from actual cache writes and costs a write on the booking hot path, while the displayed timestamp comes from a different table entirely — the next change to cache semantics has two places to update and one of them is already meaningless.

[ADVISORY] The handler throws a plain Error('Credential not found or access denied') for a failed ownership check, which tRPC wraps as INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (HTTP 500) instead of a 4xx NOT_FOUND/FORBIDDEN. Any authenticated user probing a credentialId they don't own generates 500s that pollute error monitoring as server faults, and the client's onError toast gives no signal that this is an authorization failure rather than a real server error.

[ADVISORY] The cache timestamp is formatted with a hardcoded 'en-US' Intl.DateTimeFormat inside a locale-aware component that otherwise routes all copy through t(). Non-English users see dates and times in US format (MM/DD, 12-hour) inconsistent with the rest of their localized settings UI.

[ADVISORY] The disconnect flow (mutation, confirmation dialog, success/error toasts, invalidations) is reimplemented inside this new component while the existing DisconnectIntegration component it replaces in one surface remains in use elsewhere, creating two parallel implementations of the same disconnect action. The two disconnect paths already differ in shape (this one invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars and viewer.apps.integrations; the other has its own invalidation set) and will drift further — a future change to disconnect semantics (e.g., cleanup of SelectedCalendars or cache rows) must be applied in two places, and whichever surface is forgotten ships the stale behavior.

[ADVISORY] The script uses BSD-only in-place sed syntax `sed -i '' -E`, which on GNU/Linux treats the empty string as the sed script and the s-expression as a filename, making the env update fail on non-macOS machines. Linux contributors running the new gcal-webhook test script get a sed error and GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL in ../.env is never updated, so webhook tests silently target the stale (or absent) tunnel URL; the script also resolves ENV_FILE relative to the caller's CWD ('../.env'), so it only works when invoked from exactly one directory.

[ADVISORY] The new deleteCache handler's ownership check (findFirst with userId: user.id) and the new getCacheStatusByCredentialIds groupBy have no test coverage anywhere in this diff. A regression that weakens the ownership filter (e.g., dropping the userId clause to support team credentials) would let any authenticated user delete another user's Google Calendar availability cache, forcing repeated Google API availability fetches for victims, and no test in this diff would fail.

[BUG] The availability-fetch path now performs an unconditional blanket DB write (`updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})`) that touches every SelectedCalendar row under the credential, mutating `updatedAt` timestamps that other cache/watch logic consumes — behavior beyond the PR's stated objective of 'add calendar cache status and actions'. Every availability fetch (including the booking-flow busy-time check, which runs on the hot path during scheduling) issues a write amplifying all of the user's SelectedCalendars' updatedAt. Any consumer that uses SelectedCalendar.updatedAt to judge calendar staleness or decide which calendars to re-fetch (the reason updatedAt/googleChannelId were added to the select in this same diff) now sees a 'fresh' timestamp for calendars that were never fetched, silently changing refresh cadence semantics for all calendars whenever one calendar's cache is refetched.

[BUG] The handler throws a plain `Error('Credential not found or access denied')` for the expected not-found/not-owned case, which tRPC maps to a 500 INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR instead of a 4xx the client contract implies. A stale or forged credentialId (e.g., the credential was deleted in another tab) produces a 500-level server error; the client's onError toast shows the generic 'error_deleting_cache' and server-side error monitoring is polluted with expected authorization misses logged as 500s.

[ADVISORY] The handler instantiates `CalendarCacheRepository` directly, bypassing the mock/disabled selection path this codebase maintains for calendar-cache (calendar-cache.repository.mock.ts exists precisely for disabled environments), so a `calendarCache.groupBy` query runs on every connectedCalendars load even when the calendar-cache feature is disabled. Deployments with calendar cache disabled pay an extra DB round-trip per settings-page load and the handler's behavior can no longer be swapped via the established repository-selection seam; the next change to cache-status semantics must be duplicated in both the real repository, the mock, and now this direct construction site.

[ADVISORY] The cache timestamp is formatted with a hardcoded `Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)` locale, ignoring the viewer's locale for a UI that is otherwise fully localized via useLocale(). Non-English users see the cache 'Last updated' timestamp rendered in English month/day format and labels while every other string on the card is in their locale; this ships as the only hardcoded-locale string in the component.

[ADVISORY] The shared `SelectedCalendarRepository.findMany` silently loses its `satisfies Prisma.SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs` compile-time guard in an unrelated refactor bundled into this feature PR, with no functional link to cache status. The next caller that passes a select/where key not present on the Prisma args type (e.g., a typo'd field name) will no longer be caught at compile time and will surface as a runtime Prisma error or silently dropped field in every consumer of this repository method.

[ADVISORY] The script uses the BSD/macOS-only `sed -i ''` in-place syntax, which does not perform the intended substitution under GNU sed on Linux, and resolves `ENV_FILE="../.env"` relative to the caller's CWD. On a Linux dev machine (or when run from any directory other than scripts/), the GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL is never written or is written to the wrong .env, so webhook testing silently points at a stale or missing URL instead of the fresh tunnel.

[ADVISORY] The diff adds three non-trivial server-side behaviors (deleteCache.handler mutation, getCacheStatusByCredentialIds groupBy aggregation, updateManyByCredentialId write path) and no test in the diff touches any of them. A regression in the ownership check (e.g., dropping the `userId: user.id` filter) or in the groupBy max-aggregation would let a user delete or read another user's cache status with nothing in CI to catch it; the deleteCache mutation is the first destructive calendar-cache operation exposed to end users.

[ADVISORY] The timestamp-refresh mechanism relies on Prisma bumping `@updatedAt` when `updateMany` is called with an empty `data: {}` object — a non-obvious Prisma behavior that the repository API's signature (`data: Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput`, here `{}`) does not make explicit. On a Prisma version or future upgrade where an empty data object is treated as a validation error or a no-op, either every Google availability fetch throws (breaking booking availability for all Google users) or the comment's stated intent ('Update SelectedCalendar.updatedAt') silently stops happening with no error signal.

[ADVISORY] The script treats content read from a world-writable, fixed-path /tmp/tmole.log as a trusted source for GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL, which it then writes into the app's .env without any validation. On a shared dev box or CI runner, any local process can pre-write or append a line matching the TM_KEYWORD regex (https://.*\.tunnelmole\.net) to /tmp/tmole.log; extract_url_from_log then returns the attacker's URL, and lines 63-70 (grep/sed on $ENV_FILE) persist it as GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL. Google Calendar push notifications for the developer's webhooks are then delivered to the attacker-controlled endpoint, leaking calendar event payloads; additionally, a matched URL containing a '|' character corrupts the sed s|...|...| replacement, mangling .env. A same-model variant exists at line 17: pgrep -f 'tmole 3000' blindly reuses any running tmole process regardless of which user owns it, pointing this machine's webhooks at another user's tunnel.

[BUG] The script uses BSD-only `sed -i ''` to rewrite GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL; on GNU/Linux sed fails (it parses '' as an empty script and then tries to read the s-command as a filename, erroring 'can't read'), leaving .env unmodified while the script proceeds to print '✅ Updated GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL'. A developer on Linux runs the script, sees the success checkmark, but their .env still points at the old (or missing) webhook URL — Google webhook deliveries never reach the tunnel and the gcal webhook testing session silently doesn't work.

[BUG] cleanup() ends with an unconditional `exit 0`, so every failure path that routes through it — the rate-limit branch at line 49 and the failed-URL-extraction branch at line 58 — terminates the script with a success exit status despite echoing a ❌ failure message. Any automation or wrapper invoking this script (or a developer scripting around it) observes exit code 0 and treats the webhook tunnel setup as succeeded when no tunnel URL was ever obtained, so the subsequent webhook test run fails downstream with no signal about the real cause.

[BUG] The migration backfills CalendarCache.updatedAt with DEFAULT NOW() evaluated at migration-execution time, so every pre-existing cache row is stamped with the deploy timestamp rather than any real last-update time. The new UI (connectedCalendars.handler reads _max.updatedAt and renders 'cache_last_updated') reports the deployment time as the cache's last update for all legacy rows — users see a fabricated 'just refreshed' status for cache entries that may be hours or days stale until each row is next written. Postgres evaluates the non-volatile default once during ALTER TABLE and stamps all existing rows with that single value.

[ADVISORY] The new updateManyByCredentialId call runs unconditionally after every availability fetch, outside the cache branch, issuing an UPDATE over all SelectedCalendars of the credential on the hottest calendar path even when no cache write occurred. Every Google Calendar availability check (booking pages, cron sweeps) now triggers a multi-row UPDATE on selectedCalendar, multiplying DB write load and row churn; the bumped SelectedCalendar.updatedAt is not even the value the UI displays (it reads CalendarCache.updatedAt), so the write cost is paid on every fetch regardless of whether it serves the new feature.

[ADVISORY] deleteCache.handler deletes via raw prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany, bypassing the ICalendarCacheRepository abstraction whose deleteManyByCredential implementation (and disabled-mode mock gating) already exists. Cache deletion semantics now live in two places: the repository path (gated by the calendar-cache-disabled mock) and this handler (ungated, runs even when calendar cache is disabled for the deployment, and for credentials of any app type, not just Google Calendar — the ownership check only verifies userId). The next change to cache-deletion behavior (scoping, logging, channel teardown) must be applied in both places or the paths drift.

[BUG] deleteCacheHandler throws a plain `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")` instead of a TRPCError, so a stale/nonexistent credentialId is returned to the client as a tRPC INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (500) rather than a 4xx. The user clicks 'Delete cached data' on a credential that was already removed (e.g. in another tab) and gets a generic 500-shaped failure surfaced only as the unhelpful 'error_deleting_cache' toast; the contract for an authorization/lookup miss should be NOT_FOUND/FORBIDDEN, and the raw error also masks which of the two cases fired.

[ADVISORY] The new `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` runs unconditionally after the cache-staleness if-block, so every availability fetch — including pure cache hits on booking-page loads and cron runs — issues a DB write touching all SelectedCalendars of the credential. Write amplification and row-lock contention on the availability read path (the hottest calendar path in the product), and `updatedAt` is bumped for calendars whose cache was never refreshed in that call, so if any consumer reads SelectedCalendar.updatedAt as a freshness signal it now desyncs from actual cache refreshes.

[ADVISORY] deleteCacheMutation, unlike disconnectMutation (which invalidates connectedCalendars and integrations in onSettled), performs no query invalidation and only fires the optional `onSuccess?.()` callback, so nothing guarantees the connectedCalendars query refetches after a cache deletion. After a successful delete, the dropdown keeps rendering the pre-deletion 'Last updated: <timestamp>' until some unrelated refetch happens whenever a call site omits `onSuccess`; the mutation and the visible cache status silently disagree.

[ADVISORY] The handler instantiates the concrete `CalendarCacheRepository` directly instead of going through the DI seam that swaps in `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` when calendar-cache is disabled, so the 'calendar-cache being disabled' path the mock exists for is bypassed. When the cache feature is disabled, connectedCalendars still queries the calendar_cache table on every call (the mock's skip-and-return-empty contract never applies to this new caller), and tests that rely on the mock to prove the disabled path is exercised will silently not cover this code path.

[ADVISORY] `sed -i '' -E "s|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|...|"` uses BSD/macOS-only in-place-edit syntax; on GNU/Linux sed treats the empty string as the script expression and the s-command as a filename, so the in-place env update errors out. A Linux developer running the script gets a failed GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL update while the script still prints '✅ Updated GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL in ../.Env' — the success message misreports the operation, and the webhook URL silently stays stale.

[ADVISORY] The UserWithCalendars type gains `updatedAt` and `googleChannelId` fields (and UserRepository now selects them for every user query) but nothing in this diff reads them — the cache-status enrichment in connectedCalendars.handler uses CalendarCache._max.updatedAt instead. Two different 'updated at' notions for the same connection are now plumbed into the shared connected-calendars shape with one dead on arrival; the next reader must guess which one is the real cache-status source, and the extra selected columns are carried on every user fetch for nothing.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces new security-relevant behavior in `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/calendars/deleteCache.handler.ts` (ownership check via `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })` before `calendarCache.deleteMany`) and new query logic in `packages/features/calendar-cache/calendar-cache.repository.ts` (`prisma.calendarCache.groupBy` in `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`) that is then used to enrich results in `connectedCalendars.handler.ts`. No test files or assertions are added/updated in this diff to lock in the ownership constraint or the cache-status aggregation behavior, so a future change weakening/removing `userId: user.id` would not be caught by tests added here. This is a specific, diff-grounded test-gap concern rather than a currently verifiable defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The availability-fetch path now performs an unconditional blanket DB write (`updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})`) that touches every SelectedCalendar row under the credential, mutating `updatedAt` timestamps that other cache/watch logic consumes — behavior beyond the PR's stated objective of 'add calendar cache status and actions'. Every availability fetch (including the booking-flow busy-time check, which runs on the hot path during scheduling) issues a write amplifying all of the user's SelectedCalendars' updatedAt. Any consumer that uses SelectedCalendar.updatedAt to judge calendar staleness or decide which calendars to re-fetch (the reason updatedAt/googleChannelId were added to the select in this same diff) now sees a 'fresh' timestamp for calendars that were never fetched, silently changing refresh cadence semantics for all calendars whenever one calendar's cache is refetched.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does add an unconditional write on the availability path: in `GoogleCalendarService` it always calls `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` after the fetch/cache logic. The repository method is a blanket `prisma.selectedCalendar.updateMany({ where: { credentialId }, data })`, so this will attempt to update every `SelectedCalendar` row for that credential on each invocation. Given the comment explicitly says it’s meant to update `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`, this introduces write amplification and broad timestamp-touching beyond just the calendar actually involved. However, the finding’s downstream behavioral claims (that other “cache/watch logic” consumes `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` and will now misjudge staleness/refresh cadence) aren’t directly shown in this diff, so the impact is a scope/perf/semantics concern rather than a provable brokenness from the patch alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The handler throws a plain `Error('Credential not found or access denied')` for the expected not-found/not-owned case, which tRPC maps to a 500 INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR instead of a 4xx the client contract implies. A stale or forged credentialId (e.g., the credential was deleted in another tab) produces a 500-level server error; the client's onError toast shows the generic 'error_deleting_cache' and server-side error monitoring is polluted with expected authorization misses logged as 500s.
matched_golden_ids: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate highlights that throwing a plain Error for an expected auth/not-found case causes tRPC to map it to a 500 INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, and implies it should be a 4xx/authorization-style error instead. This is the same underlying issue as the golden comment (use a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code like FORBIDDEN).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The handler instantiates `CalendarCacheRepository` directly, bypassing the mock/disabled selection path this codebase maintains for calendar-cache (calendar-cache.repository.mock.ts exists precisely for disabled environments), so a `calendarCache.groupBy` query runs on every connectedCalendars load even when the calendar-cache feature is disabled. Deployments with calendar cache disabled pay an extra DB round-trip per settings-page load and the handler's behavior can no longer be swapped via the established repository-selection seam; the next change to cache-status semantics must be duplicated in both the real repository, the mock, and now this direct construction site.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/calendars/connectedCalendars.handler.ts`, the diff adds `import { CalendarCacheRepository } ...` and then constructs it directly via `const cacheRepository = new CalendarCacheRepository();` followed by `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds(...)`, which in the real repository executes a Prisma `calendarCache.groupBy` query. The diff also shows a parallel `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` intended to no-op when calendar-cache is disabled, but this handler path does not use any factory/selection seam to choose the mock vs real implementation. That’s an architecture/scope concern (extra query + harder to swap/mock) grounded in the diff, though whether “calendar-cache is disabled” in a given deployment cannot be proven from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The cache timestamp is formatted with a hardcoded `Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)` locale, ignoring the viewer's locale for a UI that is otherwise fully localized via useLocale(). Non-English users see the cache 'Last updated' timestamp rendered in English month/day format and labels while every other string on the card is in their locale; this ships as the only hardcoded-locale string in the component.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/features/apps/components/CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx`, the timestamp is formatted with a hardcoded locale: `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" })`. This ignores the viewer’s locale (despite the component using `useLocale()` for strings), causing non-English users to see an English/US-formatted date/time for the cache timestamp.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The shared `SelectedCalendarRepository.findMany` silently loses its `satisfies Prisma.SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs` compile-time guard in an unrelated refactor bundled into this feature PR, with no functional link to cache status. The next caller that passes a select/where key not present on the Prisma args type (e.g., a typo'd field name) will no longer be caught at compile time and will surface as a runtime Prisma error or silently dropped field in every consumer of this repository method.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does remove `satisfies Prisma.SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs` in `SelectedCalendarRepository.findMany`, but the replacement still passes an object literal directly into `prisma.selectedCalendar.findMany({ where, select, orderBy })`, which is itself type-checked against Prisma’s `findMany` argument type. This change does not verifiably eliminate compile-time checking for invalid top-level Prisma args. Also, the cited risk about typo’d field names inside `where/select` is not something the removed `satisfies` necessarily guaranteed anyway (it depends on how `where/select` are typed upstream, which isn’t shown).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The script uses the BSD/macOS-only `sed -i ''` in-place syntax, which does not perform the intended substitution under GNU sed on Linux, and resolves `ENV_FILE="../.env"` relative to the caller's CWD. On a Linux dev machine (or when run from any directory other than scripts/), the GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL is never written or is written to the wrong .env, so webhook testing silently points at a stale or missing URL instead of the fresh tunnel.

adjudication.rationale: The newly added `scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh` hardcodes `ENV_FILE="../.env"`, which is resolved relative to the caller’s current working directory (not the script’s directory). If run from repo root as `scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh`, it will target `../.env` (outside the repo) and thus update the wrong file. Additionally, it uses `sed -i '' -E ...`, which is the BSD/macOS in-place syntax and is not reliably compatible with GNU sed on Linux, risking the substitution not being applied.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The diff adds three non-trivial server-side behaviors (deleteCache.handler mutation, getCacheStatusByCredentialIds groupBy aggregation, updateManyByCredentialId write path) and no test in the diff touches any of them. A regression in the ownership check (e.g., dropping the `userId: user.id` filter) or in the groupBy max-aggregation would let a user delete or read another user's cache status with nothing in CI to catch it; the deleteCache mutation is the first destructive calendar-cache operation exposed to end users.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces new server-side logic paths without any accompanying test changes: (1) a new destructive TRPC mutation `viewer.calendars.deleteCache` wired in `_router.tsx` and implemented in `deleteCache.handler.ts` with an ownership check (`credential.findFirst` with `userId: user.id`) and `calendarCache.deleteMany`; (2) new repository aggregation `CalendarCacheRepository.getCacheStatusByCredentialIds()` using `prisma.calendarCache.groupBy(... _max.updatedAt ...)` and its usage in `connectedCalendars.handler.ts` to add `cacheUpdatedAt`; and (3) a new write path `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId()` called from `GoogleCalendarService` to update many rows. No test files are added/updated in the diff to validate the ownership guard or the correctness of the groupBy/max mapping, so regressions (e.g., removing the `userId` filter or mis-aggregating status) would not be caught in CI.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The timestamp-refresh mechanism relies on Prisma bumping `@updatedAt` when `updateMany` is called with an empty `data: {}` object — a non-obvious Prisma behavior that the repository API's signature (`data: Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput`, here `{}`) does not make explicit. On a Prisma version or future upgrade where an empty data object is treated as a validation error or a no-op, either every Google availability fetch throws (breaking booking availability for all Google users) or the comment's stated intent ('Update SelectedCalendar.updatedAt') silently stops happening with no error signal.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `GoogleCalendarService` calling `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` with an intentionally empty `data` object and a comment claiming it will "Update SelectedCalendar.updatedAt". The repository method signature (`data: Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput`) doesn’t communicate that `{}` is a special/required usage, and the behavior depends on how Prisma handles empty `updateMany` payloads and whether it bumps `@updatedAt` without any explicit field change. From the diff alone we can verify the change introduces a fragile, non-obvious dependency on Prisma semantics, but we cannot verify that it currently throws or is currently a no-op in this repo’s Prisma version.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The script treats content read from a world-writable, fixed-path /tmp/tmole.log as a trusted source for GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL, which it then writes into the app's .env without any validation. On a shared dev box or CI runner, any local process can pre-write or append a line matching the TM_KEYWORD regex (https://.*\.tunnelmole\.net) to /tmp/tmole.log; extract_url_from_log then returns the attacker's URL, and lines 63-70 (grep/sed on $ENV_FILE) persist it as GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL. Google Calendar push notifications for the developer's webhooks are then delivered to the attacker-controlled endpoint, leaking calendar event payloads; additionally, a matched URL containing a '|' character corrupts the sed s|...|...| replacement, mangling .env. A same-model variant exists at line 17: pgrep -f 'tmole 3000' blindly reuses any running tmole process regardless of which user owns it, pointing this machine's webhooks at another user's tunnel.

adjudication.rationale: The newly added `scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh` hardcodes `LOG_FILE="/tmp/tmole.log"` and then trusts its contents via `extract_url_from_log()` (grep/head) to set `TUNNEL_URL`, which is persisted into `../.env` as `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` (lines updating with `sed`/`echo`). Because `/tmp` is world-writable and the script reuses an existing log file/process (`pgrep -f "tmole $TM_PORT"` + `extract_url_from_log`), another local process could pre-populate/append a matching `https://.*\.tunnelmole\.net` line and cause the script to write an attacker-controlled webhook URL. The `sed` substitution also uses `|` as a delimiter without escaping, so a matched string containing `|` would break/mangle the `.env` update.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The script uses BSD-only `sed -i ''` to rewrite GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL; on GNU/Linux sed fails (it parses '' as an empty script and then tries to read the s-command as a filename, erroring 'can't read'), leaving .env unmodified while the script proceeds to print '✅ Updated GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL'. A developer on Linux runs the script, sees the success checkmark, but their .env still points at the old (or missing) webhook URL — Google webhook deliveries never reach the tunnel and the gcal webhook testing session silently doesn't work.
matched_golden_ids: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that the script uses BSD/macOS-specific `sed -i ''` syntax, which fails on GNU/Linux sed, matching the golden issue about macOS-specific sed inline-edit syntax breaking on Linux.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] cleanup() ends with an unconditional `exit 0`, so every failure path that routes through it — the rate-limit branch at line 49 and the failed-URL-extraction branch at line 58 — terminates the script with a success exit status despite echoing a ❌ failure message. Any automation or wrapper invoking this script (or a developer scripting around it) observes exit code 0 and treats the webhook tunnel setup as succeeded when no tunnel URL was ever obtained, so the subsequent webhook test run fails downstream with no signal about the real cause.

adjudication.rationale: In `scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh`, the `cleanup()` function always ends with `exit 0`. Both the rate-limit failure path (`if grep -q "limited to 10 tunnels per hour" ...; then ... cleanup`) and the “Failed to extract Tunnelmole URL” path (`if [ -z "$TUNNEL_URL" ]; then ... cleanup`) invoke `cleanup()`, so the script exits with a success status even after printing a ❌ error. This can mislead automation/wrappers into treating the run as successful when it actually failed to obtain a tunnel URL.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The migration backfills CalendarCache.updatedAt with DEFAULT NOW() evaluated at migration-execution time, so every pre-existing cache row is stamped with the deploy timestamp rather than any real last-update time. The new UI (connectedCalendars.handler reads _max.updatedAt and renders 'cache_last_updated') reports the deployment time as the cache's last update for all legacy rows — users see a fabricated 'just refreshed' status for cache entries that may be hours or days stale until each row is next written. Postgres evaluates the non-volatile default once during ALTER TABLE and stamps all existing rows with that single value.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `CalendarCache.updatedAt` with `DEFAULT NOW()` in the migration (`ALTER TABLE "CalendarCache" ADD COLUMN "updatedAt" ... DEFAULT NOW();`) and also sets the Prisma field to `@default(now()) @updatedAt`. The new UI path (`connectedCalendars.handler.ts`) reads `prisma.calendarCache.groupBy(... _max: { updatedAt: true })` and displays it as `cache_last_updated`. For pre-existing rows, the migration will populate `updatedAt` with the default at migration time (not a historical “last refreshed” value), so legacy caches will appear freshly updated until those rows are next written. This is a real behavior/UX correctness issue introduced by the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new updateManyByCredentialId call runs unconditionally after every availability fetch, outside the cache branch, issuing an UPDATE over all SelectedCalendars of the credential on the hottest calendar path even when no cache write occurred. Every Google Calendar availability check (booking pages, cron sweeps) now triggers a multi-row UPDATE on selectedCalendar, multiplying DB write load and row churn; the bumped SelectedCalendar.updatedAt is not even the value the UI displays (it reads CalendarCache.updatedAt), so the write cost is paid on every fetch regardless of whether it serves the new feature.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an unconditional `await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {});` in `CalendarService.ts` after the cache-write block, so it will execute on every availability refresh regardless of whether caching happened. Since `updateManyByCredentialId` calls `prisma.selectedCalendar.updateMany({ where: { credentialId }, data })`, this can introduce extra DB write work/row churn on a hot path. Also, the new UI cache status is sourced from `CalendarCache.updatedAt` via `CalendarCacheRepository.getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` and `connectedCalendars.handler.ts`, not from `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`, so the justification for touching `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` is not evident in this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] deleteCache.handler deletes via raw prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany, bypassing the ICalendarCacheRepository abstraction whose deleteManyByCredential implementation (and disabled-mode mock gating) already exists. Cache deletion semantics now live in two places: the repository path (gated by the calendar-cache-disabled mock) and this handler (ungated, runs even when calendar cache is disabled for the deployment, and for credentials of any app type, not just Google Calendar — the ownership check only verifies userId). The next change to cache-deletion behavior (scoping, logging, channel teardown) must be applied in both places or the paths drift.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `deleteCache.handler.ts` directly calling `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany({ where: { credentialId } })` after only an ownership check (`prisma.credential.findFirst` with `id` + `userId`). This bypasses the existing `ICalendarCacheRepository` abstraction, which already has `deleteManyByCredential` and a disabled-mode mock (`CalendarCacheRepositoryMock.deleteManyByCredential()` logs and does nothing). As a result, cache deletion semantics are now split between repository-based paths and this new TRPC handler, increasing drift risk for future changes (scoping, side effects, logging). The claim about “runs even when calendar cache is disabled” is plausible given the mock, but the mechanism that swaps in the mock isn’t shown in the diff, so this is primarily an architecture/single-source-of-truth concern rather than a provable defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] deleteCacheHandler throws a plain `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")` instead of a TRPCError, so a stale/nonexistent credentialId is returned to the client as a tRPC INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (500) rather than a 4xx. The user clicks 'Delete cached data' on a credential that was already removed (e.g. in another tab) and gets a generic 500-shaped failure surfaced only as the unhelpful 'error_deleting_cache' toast; the contract for an authorization/lookup miss should be NOT_FOUND/FORBIDDEN, and the raw error also masks which of the two cases fired.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/calendars/deleteCache.handler.ts`, the handler does `throw new Error("Credential not found or access denied")` when the credential lookup fails. In tRPC, throwing a plain `Error` is typically converted into an `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` response, so an expected 4xx condition (not found / forbidden due to `id` not belonging to `user.id`) will be surfaced as a 500 to the client. This is directly verifiable from the diff and matches the described stale/nonexistent `credentialId` case.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` runs unconditionally after the cache-staleness if-block, so every availability fetch — including pure cache hits on booking-page loads and cron runs — issues a DB write touching all SelectedCalendars of the credential. Write amplification and row-lock contention on the availability read path (the hottest calendar path in the product), and `updatedAt` is bumped for calendars whose cache was never refreshed in that call, so if any consumer reads SelectedCalendar.updatedAt as a freshness signal it now desyncs from actual cache refreshes.

adjudication.rationale: In `GoogleCalendarService` the diff adds `await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {});` *after* the cache-refresh conditional block, so it will execute on every call to that method regardless of whether `fetchAvailability`/`setAvailabilityInCache` ran. `updateManyByCredentialId` is implemented as a Prisma `updateMany` over all `selectedCalendar` rows for the credential, which can introduce unnecessary write/lock work on a hot availability path and can bump `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` even when no cache refresh occurred (consistent with the added comment). The broader claim about “booking-page loads and cron runs” being affected depends on call sites not shown, but the unconditional mass update itself is directly shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] deleteCacheMutation, unlike disconnectMutation (which invalidates connectedCalendars and integrations in onSettled), performs no query invalidation and only fires the optional `onSuccess?.()` callback, so nothing guarantees the connectedCalendars query refetches after a cache deletion. After a successful delete, the dropdown keeps rendering the pre-deletion 'Last updated: <timestamp>' until some unrelated refetch happens whenever a call site omits `onSuccess`; the mutation and the visible cache status silently disagree.

adjudication.rationale: In `CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx`, `deleteCacheMutation` only shows a toast and calls the optional `onSuccess?.()`; it does not invalidate any tRPC/react-query caches (unlike `disconnectMutation`, which explicitly invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` and `utils.viewer.apps.integrations` in `onSettled`). Since `connectedCalendars.handler.ts` now enriches each calendar with `cacheUpdatedAt`, deleting cache via `deleteCache.handler.ts` changes the data that `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` would return, so without an explicit invalidation inside the mutation, the UI can remain stale unless the caller-provided `onSuccess` happens to trigger a refetch. The diff shows this reliance on an optional callback, but does not show whether all call sites always refetch.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The handler instantiates the concrete `CalendarCacheRepository` directly instead of going through the DI seam that swaps in `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` when calendar-cache is disabled, so the 'calendar-cache being disabled' path the mock exists for is bypassed. When the cache feature is disabled, connectedCalendars still queries the calendar_cache table on every call (the mock's skip-and-return-empty contract never applies to this new caller), and tests that rely on the mock to prove the disabled path is exercised will silently not cover this code path.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/calendars/connectedCalendars.handler.ts`, the new logic `import { CalendarCacheRepository } ...` and `const cacheRepository = new CalendarCacheRepository();` directly constructs the concrete Prisma-backed repository and immediately calls `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds(...)`, which performs a `prisma.calendarCache.groupBy(...)`. The diff also shows an `ICalendarCacheRepository` interface and a `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` whose methods explicitly log “Skipping ... due to calendar-cache being disabled” and return empty results. Because this new call site does not go through any DI seam or factory visible in the diff, it will always hit the DB-backed implementation from this handler, making the mock/disabled behavior unreachable from this path and potentially undermining tests or intended “disabled” behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] `sed -i '' -E "s|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|...|"` uses BSD/macOS-only in-place-edit syntax; on GNU/Linux sed treats the empty string as the script expression and the s-command as a filename, so the in-place env update errors out. A Linux developer running the script gets a failed GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL update while the script still prints '✅ Updated GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL in ../.Env' — the success message misreports the operation, and the webhook URL silently stays stale.

adjudication.rationale: In `scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh`, the env update path uses `sed -i '' -E "s|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|...|"` which is the BSD/macOS in-place syntax. On GNU/Linux, `-i ''` is not interpreted the same way and commonly causes the substitution to fail (treating `''`/next token unexpectedly), yet the script unconditionally prints `✅ Updated GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL...` right after the sed invocation with no error check. This can lead to broken behavior for Linux developers: the variable is not updated while the script reports success.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The UserWithCalendars type gains `updatedAt` and `googleChannelId` fields (and UserRepository now selects them for every user query) but nothing in this diff reads them — the cache-status enrichment in connectedCalendars.handler uses CalendarCache._max.updatedAt instead. Two different 'updated at' notions for the same connection are now plumbed into the shared connected-calendars shape with one dead on arrival; the next reader must guess which one is the real cache-status source, and the extra selected columns are carried on every user fetch for nothing.

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly expands `UserWithCalendars` to include `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` and `googleChannelId` (packages/lib/getConnectedDestinationCalendars.ts) and updates `UserRepository` to select those columns (packages/lib/server/repository/user.ts), but the new cache-status feature shown here uses `CalendarCache._max.updatedAt` via `CalendarCacheRepository.getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` and plumbs that into a separate `cacheUpdatedAt` field (connectedCalendars.handler.ts). Nothing in this diff consumes the newly selected `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`/`googleChannelId`, so the finding about redundant selection / potential confusion between two “updated at” concepts is supported by the changes shown, though it’s not a correctness bug by itself.
